newsletter_intro: Wine labels can feel like they’re trying a little too hard sometimes. But once you know what to look for, they get a lot less mysterious and a whole lot more useful. Let’s make label-reading feel simple.

instagram_carousel.caption:
Wine labels can feel a little like they’re speaking another language. But once you know the difference between Old World and New World labels, a lot of the confusion starts to disappear.

I broke down the main things to look for — from grape vs. place, to vintage, ABV, and a few label terms that actually mean something. If you’ve ever stood in the wine aisle feeling lost, this one’s for you. 🍷

What’s the label term you always have to look up?

instagram_reel.hook: If wine labels make you feel confused, you are absolutely not alone.
instagram_reel.script:
If wine labels make you feel confused, you are absolutely not alone. A lot of them are basically giving you information… just not in a very friendly way.

Here’s the simple version: Old World wines usually lead with place, while New World wines usually lead with the grape. So if you see Burgundy or Chianti, that’s region-first. If you see Cabernet Sauvignon or Chardonnay front and centre, that’s grape-first.

Then look for the vintage, which is the harvest year, and ABV, which tells you the alcohol level and can give you a clue about body and style.

And if you see words like Reserva or Lees, don’t panic. They actually mean something useful. You do not need to memorize every label in the wine aisle — just start with the basics.

Wine labels are not trying to be helpful on purpose — but I can make them make sense.

The biggest thing to know is this: Old World wines usually tell you the place first, and New World wines usually tell you the grape first. So Burgundy or Chianti? That’s more about region. Cabernet Sauvignon or Chardonnay on the front? That’s the grape.

Then check the vintage — that’s the year the grapes were harvested — and ABV, which gives you a clue about how light or full the wine might be.

If you see words like Reserva, Classico, or lees, those are not random fancy words. They actually tell you something useful.

You do not need to know everything. Just learn the basics and let the label work for you.

linkedin.post:
Wine labels can be intimidating, but they are actually one of the most useful tools a shopper has.

The biggest shift comes from understanding the difference between Old World and New World labeling. In many European regions, the label is built around place. In many New World regions, the grape variety is front and centre. That one distinction clears up a lot of confusion for consumers.

From there, simple details like vintage, ABV, and common terms such as Reserva or lees can help guide expectations about style, structure, and aging.

For brands, retailers, and hospitality teams, the opportunity is clear: the more approachable we make wine language, the more confident people feel making a purchase.

Wine does not need to be exclusive to be credible. It just needs to be understandable.
